text:
Slight problem: Tin Snips DON’T come in left or right handed. The 3 types, come in three basic colors for cutting direction!
Red handles – Used to make “left” or counterclockwise cuts in sheet metal.
Green handles – Used to make “right” or clockwise cuts in sheet metal.
Yellow handles – Used for straight cuts in sheet metal.

Unless your views are cutting circles, the NED the Yellow Handle (Straight) cutting snips.

text: Interesting how easy it is to gloss over the fundamental questions that one has as a beginner by assuming it is already known. Whilst it is probably easier to go from breadboard to tracked perfboard (by basically replicating the same layout) to avoid making wiring errors in construction it is almost a quantum leap to go from breadboard to single pad perfboard without taking time to optimize the layout more efficiently & effectively. I recently found a video that tackled this issue by looking at grouping the nodes in the circuit and using vertical jumper wires on the top to connect the tracks and horizontal wiring & solder tracks on the back to connect component wiring. By studying this layout it is possible to compress the number of rows & columns holes that are needed on a pad perfboard circuit.

author: @MarcdeVinck

text: Depends on your project. A 'typical' breadboard has some holes connected allowing for multiple components to connect together faster. You may have to either jump between pads, or cut some traces to build your circuit. A "donut" board has 1 pad per hole. None of the holes are connected. I like 'donut' boards for freeform circuits and 'typical' breadboards when working with ICs since you can easily break out the pins to multiple components. Hope that helps!
